questions.prompt: A maize farm supports grasshoppers, lizards, hawks and earthworms alongside the maize plants.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: (a) An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with their non-living (physical) environment as a functional unit. (b) Producer: maize plants. Consumers: grasshopper (primary), lizard and hawk (secondary). (c) Maize → grasshopper → lizard → hawk (any three-linked correct sequence earns full marks). (d) Lizards and hawks would lose a food source and decline, while maize yield would rise without the pest; the food chain would be disrupted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term ecosystem.
parts.correctAnswer: An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with one another and with their non-living (physical) environment as a functional unit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the producer and two primary or secondary consumers in the farm community.
parts.correctAnswer: Producer: maize plants. Consumers: grasshopper (primary), lizard and hawk (secondary).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Construct a food chain using three of the organisms named above.
parts.correctAnswer: Maize → grasshopper → lizard → hawk (any three-linked correct sequence earns full marks).

parts.label: d
parts.text: State and explain one effect on the ecosystem if all the grasshoppers were removed.
parts.correctAnswer: Lizards and hawks would lose a food source and decline, while maize yield would rise without the pest; the food chain would be disrupted.

questions.prompt: A mixture contains iron filings, sand and common salt.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: (a) Pass a magnet over or through the mixture; the iron filings are attracted to the magnet, leaving sand and salt behind. (b) Add water and stir to dissolve the salt, filter to remove the sand, then evaporate (or crystallise) the filtrate to obtain pure salt. (c) Dissolved salt particles are too small and pass through the pores of filter paper with the water; only insoluble solids are trapped. (d) Distillation: the water is evaporated and then condensed back to pure liquid, leaving the salt behind.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the iron filings can be separated from the mixture.
parts.correctAnswer: Pass a magnet over or through the mixture; the iron filings are attracted to the magnet, leaving sand and salt behind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Outline the steps you would use to obtain pure salt from the remaining mixture.
parts.correctAnswer: Add water and stir to dissolve the salt, filter to remove the sand, then evaporate (or crystallise) the filtrate to obtain pure salt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why filtration alone cannot separate the dissolved salt from the water.
parts.correctAnswer: Dissolved salt particles are too small and pass through the pores of filter paper with the water; only insoluble solids are trapped.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the process you would use to recover pure water from the salt solution.
parts.correctAnswer: Distillation: the water is evaporated and then condensed back to pure liquid, leaving the salt behind.

questions.prompt: A student connects a battery and two identical lamps in series to form a closed circuit.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: (a) Battery (supplies electrical energy), connecting wires (carry current), lamps (convert electrical energy to light), and a switch (opens or closes the circuit). (b) There is only one path for the charge to flow, so the same quantity of charge passes every point per second. (c) The lamps become dimmer because total resistance increases, so the current through each lamp decreases. (d) In series, resistances add: R = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 Ω.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the components needed for the circuit and state the function of each.
parts.correctAnswer: Battery (supplies electrical energy), connecting wires (carry current), lamps (convert electrical energy to light), and a switch (opens or closes the circuit).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
parts.correctAnswer: There is only one path for the charge to flow, so the same quantity of charge passes every point per second.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State and explain what happens to the brightness of the lamps when a third identical lamp is added in series.
parts.correctAnswer: The lamps become dimmer because total resistance increases, so the current through each lamp decreases.

parts.label: d
parts.text: If each lamp has a resistance of 4 Ω, calculate the total resistance when three lamps are connected in series.
parts.correctAnswer: In series, resistances add: R = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 Ω.

questions.prompt: A meal of kenkey and fried fish is eaten by a student.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: (a) Digestion is the breakdown of large, insoluble food molecules into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream. (b) Salivary amylase (ptyalin), which acts on starch, breaking it down to maltose. (c) Protein digestion begins in the stomach, where pepsin breaks proteins into peptides in the presence of hydrochloric acid. (d) Its inner wall is folded into millions of villi (with microvilli), giving a very large surface area, and each villus has a rich blood supply and thin walls for fast diffusion.

parts.correctAnswer: Salivary amylase (ptyalin), which acts on starch, breaking it down to maltose.

parts.label: c

parts.label: d

questions.prompt: A farmer wants to improve a patch of land before planting maize.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: (a) Mineral particles (anchor roots and supply nutrients) and humus/organic matter (holds moisture and releases nutrients); air and water in the pores support root respiration and nutrient uptake. (b) Loam balances sand, silt and clay with humus, so it drains well yet retains enough water and nutrients, and it is easily worked by roots and tools. (c) Compost adds humus, which improves soil structure and water retention and releases nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium slowly as it decomposes. (d) Contour ploughing (or terracing): ploughing across the slope slows run-off, reducing soil erosion and keeping nutrients in place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two components of soil and state the importance of each to plant growth.
parts.correctAnswer: Mineral particles (anchor roots and supply nutrients) and humus/organic matter (holds moisture and releases nutrients); air and water in the pores support root respiration and nutrient uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why loamy soil is considered best for crop production.
parts.correctAnswer: Loam balances sand, silt and clay with humus, so it drains well yet retains enough water and nutrients, and it is easily worked by roots and tools.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how adding compost improves the soil.
parts.correctAnswer: Compost adds humus, which improves soil structure and water retention and releases nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium slowly as it decomposes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one soil conservation practice the farmer can use on sloping land and explain how it works.
parts.correctAnswer: Contour ploughing (or terracing): ploughing across the slope slows run-off, reducing soil erosion and keeping nutrients in place.

questions.prompt: Your community is facing a waste disposal crisis. Discuss four proper methods of managing solid waste in your community, giving one advantage and one limitation of each method.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: A strong answer discusses four of: sanitary landfilling (advantage: handles large mixed volumes cheaply; limitation: needs land and can pollute groundwater if unlined), composting of organic waste (advantage: produces manure and reduces refuse volume; limitation: only organic fraction and needs sorting), recycling and reuse (advantage: conserves raw materials and creates income; limitation: requires separation at source and markets for recyclables), and controlled incineration (advantage: greatly reduces volume and destroys pathogens; limitation: smoke and air pollution, high cost). Each method is described clearly, and one advantage and one limitation are explicitly tied to community conditions such as cost, land or labour.

questions.prompt: Discuss the causes and effects of water pollution in Ghanaian communities and suggest two measures that can be taken to control it.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Integrated Science Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: A strong answer names causes such as dumping of refuse and sewage into streams, chemical fertiliser and pesticide run-off from farms, illegal mining (galamsey) washing mercury and silt into rivers, and oil or soapy water from washing at riverbanks. Effects include water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid, death of fish and other aquatic life as oxygen levels fall, siltation that raises the cost of treating pipe-borne water, and loss of fishing livelihoods. Control measures: enforcing by-laws and pollution penalties with regular monitoring of water bodies, and educating communities while providing proper refuse collection so waste is not dumped into rivers; buffer-zone tree planting along riverbanks is also creditable.

Explains at least three effects on health, aquatic life or livelihoods
Suggests two workable control measures

questions.prompt: Explain four ways by which the 1992 Constitution of Ghana promotes democracy in the country.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Social Studies Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: A strong answer explains four of: separation of powers among the Executive, Legislature and Judiciary so no arm dominates; the Bill of Rights (fundamental human rights in Chapter 5) protecting freedoms of speech, association and movement; provision for periodic, universal-suffrage elections through an independent Electoral Commission; an independent judiciary empowered to review and strike down unconstitutional acts; and recognition of a multi-party system allowing competition for power. Each point is developed to show the democratic principle it serves, with examples such as peaceful changes of government through elections.

questions.prompt: Discuss four causes of electoral violence in Ghana and suggest two measures that can be taken to prevent it.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Social Studies Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: Credible causes include: winner-takes-all politics, which raises the stakes of every election; mistrust of the Electoral Commission or security agencies by losing parties; the activities of party militias and vigilante groups; ethnic or religious campaigning that inflames divisions; and youth unemployment, which makes young people available for paid violence. Preventive measures: continuous voter and peace education by the NCCE, civil society and religious bodies, and firm, impartial enforcement of the law against vigilante groups together with dialogue platforms such as the National Peace Council bringing parties to sign peace pacts. Each cause must be tied to the mechanism by which it produces violence.

questions.prompt: Discuss four negative effects of rural-urban migration on the rural communities the migrants leave behind.

questions.workedSolution: A strong answer keeps the focus on the sending community: loss of energetic young labour, which lowers farm output and leaves agriculture to the aged; depopulation, which makes schools and clinics lose enrolment and staff and can lead to their closure; breakdown of extended-family care, leaving children and the elderly without support; and slower local development as the most educated and enterprising residents leave. questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Social Studies Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: Creditable strategies: teaching Ghanaian languages, history and cultural studies in schools so children internalize them early; deliberate family transmission — parents speaking mother tongues at home and involving children in festivals, naming ceremonies and storytelling; documentation and promotion through museums, cultural centres and media; and state support for festivals, traditional authorities and creative arts that keep crafts, music and dance economically viable. questions.prompt: Discuss four causes of teenage pregnancy in Ghana and explain two effects it has on the girl's education.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Social Studies Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: Creditable causes: poverty, which pushes girls into transactional relationships for basic needs; inadequate sexuality education at home and school; peer pressure and exposure to explicit media; and broken homes or weak parental supervision. Educational effects: many girls drop out or are withdrawn, cutting short their schooling and qualifications; even where re-entry is possible, pregnancy and childcare interrupt learning, lower performance and narrow future career options. The best answers treat the subject sensitively, avoid blame, and show how the causes interact with economic circumstances.

questions.prompt: Discuss four effects of illegal mining (galamsey) on the environment in Ghana and suggest two measures to control the practice.
questions.contentLabel: Original BrillaPrep curriculum-aligned WASSCE Social Studies Paper 2 theory practice; not official WAEC examination material. Use the enabled feedback channel to report corrections.
questions.workedSolution: Environmental effects: pollution and siltation of rivers such as the Pra and Ankobra, making water unusable and costly to treat; destruction of forest cover and cocoa farms as land is excavated; mercury and chemical contamination of soil and water, poisoning fish and entering food chains; and abandoned pits that breed mosquitoes and cause deadly accidents. Control measures: strict, impartial enforcement of mining laws with prosecution of financiers, not only labourers; provision of regulated small-scale mining zones with training in safer methods; and sustained public education plus reclamation of mined-out land with tree planting. Each effect is tied to its environmental mechanism.
